sections.title: Keystones
sections.intro: The calls that set how a mystery works in WOTR at all: how much the reader may solve, the fair-play terms, when secrets pay, what knowing costs, what catching a lie means, and how a case plays at the table against the page.

questions.title: How much the reader may solve
questions.question: In written work, does the reader stand ahead of the investigator, beside him, or does each book choose?
questions.context: R5-C1 defaults to writing 'from whoever knows least'. Isaac's own manuscripts run dramatic irony (the reader knows what a character does not): the Greyshaft Nine coldhouse shown in full, then Wystan's catch. The Golden Age puzzle (the interwar fair-play novel) and honkaku (Japan's 'orthodox' fair-play mystery) keep the villain's room shut so the reader can race the detective.

options.label: Reader ahead, inverted
options.consequence: The villain's room is shown; the reader knows who and how, and the pleasure is the catch and its cost (the inverted mystery, Columbo's form). R5-C1's least-knowing default narrows to the investigator's own scenes.

options.label: Reader beside, fair puzzle
options.consequence: The villain's room stays shut until the solution; the reader holds exactly what the investigator holds and may beat him to it. Cutaways to the other side end inside a mystery.

options.label: Each book declares
options.consequence: Each book or thread bible names its mode: inverted, fair puzzle, or the split (the reader knows who, never how or why). Undeclared work defaults to inverted, the house mode.

questions.rec_reason: Isaac's own work is inverted and the night-watch book is built on it, but Mother of Learning and Lord of the Mysteries show the reader racing the hero pays too; a declared mode keeps each book honest about which game it plays.

questions.title: The fair-play terms
questions.question: Which fair-play terms become law for every mystery, written or played?
questions.context: R48-30 wants surprises 'a player could have caught', and R71-30 has the notes list each planted sign, for fights only. Ronald Knox's 1929 commandments and S. S. Van Dine's 1928 rules bar unseen clues and the 'undiscovered poison' explained by a lecture. Magic already breaks Knox's ban on the supernatural, so WOTR needs its own terms.

options.label: Nothing unseen
options.consequence: The solution rests only on what the reader or player was shown. A clue the investigator held and the page withheld voids the solution; the notes list every clue used.

options.label: Codex-backed solutions
options.consequence: Any working in a solution has a Codex line and its rule acted on the page first. No working is invented to solve a case; one that falsifies perception is planted (R71-30) or barred.

options.label: Sealed solution
options.consequence: The truth (who, how, why) is written in the notes before the first clue is placed and never moves to fit a guess: R57-10's ban on rigging made a procedure.

options.label: A challenge mark
options.consequence: Ellery Queen's device: a book marks the point where every clue is on the page, as a chapter-head line or a set-off notice, before the solution.

questions.rec_reason: These three are his fair abilities with findable counters applied to secrets, and B is Knox's undiscovered poison rewritten for a world with magic; the challenge mark is a parlour game that breaks the chancery's flat voice.

questions.title: When secrets pay
questions.question: How often does a thread pay one of its secrets, and may one stay unpaid for good?
questions.context: Nothing rules it. R70-17 lets a scene break off so 'the next scene owes what was withheld'; R47-12 keeps the world's own mysteries open. The night-watch book's chapter-ten audit found 23 open hooks, seven dormant. The one-word letter in Isaac's Part 16 is the archive's only secret kept from the reader as well.

options.label: Something every session
options.consequence: Each session pays one piece of an open secret, small or large, the web-serial way (a hook paid every instalment); no secret lies dormant past two sessions without a new sign, and every secret pays.

options.label: Caught or clocked
options.consequence: A secret pays when his PC catches it or its Front (a faction's clock of moves) resolves, never on a timer. A few are marked 'kept' and never pay on the page, as the one-word letter.

options.label: Big ones at arc ends
options.consequence: Small pieces pay whenever caught; the large secrets (a hidden hand, a true parentage) pay only at an arc's end, staged as set pieces, and none is kept for good.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the solve in Isaac's hands and lets the Fronts pay what he misses, and a kept secret or two is what makes the rest of the world feel deep.

questions.title: What knowing costs
questions.question: Is knowledge itself dangerous in WOTR, and through what?
questions.context: Canon prices contact only: Wystan carries 'forty-one minutes belonging to other people' after an Anamnetic read (bare fingers on a residue), and one artificer spent his last months insisting on a name not his. Lord of the Mysteries lets names and texts harm their reader, but its hidden world cannot carry where magic is 'gatekept by administration' (R60-13). Fear's toll on the mind is the Horror section's.

options.label: Only contact costs
options.consequence: As now: knowing is safe, and bare-fingered contact with a residue is the one priced act. Forbidden texts are dangerous only because the Gate (the licensing of magic) punishes holding them.

options.label: Being known to know
options.consequence: The danger is who notices: the Gate punishes unlicensed knowledge, The Mother reads the Watch's inserts, a witness becomes a target. Every secret learned opens a Ledger line on who knows he knows.

options.label: Records that act
options.consequence: B, plus a few records act on whoever touches them through canon mechanism (Mnemata, records held in objects, R61-70), priced by Resilience with the counter named in the notes. No invented figure.

options.label: Names that call
options.consequence: C, plus speaking certain true names draws the owner's attention, the Lord of the Mysteries device, given a WOTR mechanism and a findable counter before it is ever used.

questions.rec_reason: Isaac picked the Lord of the Mysteries register, and C gives its dangerous texts on mechanism canon already has, with a counter; D's named attention has no physics under it yet and would need new canon before its first use.

questions.title: What catching a lie is
questions.question: What counts as catching an NPC's lie?
questions.context: Table Rule 8 keeps a wrong NPC statement 'uncorrected until he catches it', and R48-42 says 'the player has to catch them'; neither says what catching is. Isaac is author and player at once, and R71-6 makes the read his. How many lies a session carries is the table questionnaire's; what an uncaught lie becomes is MY10.

options.label: His PC acts on it
options.consequence: Caught when his PC acts on the truth or names the lie in play. Isaac spotting it in chat changes nothing in the world until his PC moves.

options.label: Isaac names it
options.consequence: Caught when Isaac names it, in character or out. The notes mark it caught; the NPC learns only what his PC did or said.

options.label: A fact on the page
options.consequence: Caught once a fact that breaks it is on the page, taken up or not; Natalie's duty ends when she places it.

questions.rec_reason: The world answers what his PC does, which keeps what Isaac knows as author from leaking into his PC, and acting on the truth is how a player shows he caught it.

questions.title: Finding clues at the table
questions.question: When Isaac's PC searches, how are clues found?
questions.context: R71-6 has Natalie place the tell and 'never draws the conclusion'; R48-48 explains only when asked. GUMSHOE (Robin Laws's investigation system for tabletop play) rules that the right look always finds the core clue, so the drama is reading it. Older tabletop makes finding the test, and a missed clue stays missed.

options.label: The right look finds
options.consequence: GUMSHOE whole: his PC looking in the right place with the right means finds every clue there; nothing hides behind luck or phrasing.

options.label: Only the right question
options.consequence: A clue is found only when Isaac names where to look or what to test; a vague search finds the room's surface, and missed clues stay missed.

options.label: Core found, extras earned
options.consequence: Each conclusion's core clue comes to any sensible look; the further clues that sharpen it, speed it or name the purse (who paid) come only to the right question or instrument.

questions.rec_reason: It never strands a case on phrasing, and it still rewards Isaac for reading the Standing Inventory the way the archive's best clues (oil where tallow burns) demand.

questions.title: Cutting away inside a case
questions.question: While Isaac's PC works a case, may a turn cut away to the other side?
questions.context: R49-09 lets a turn close on 'an NPC plotting', and R71-52 makes an ambush's shooter half a closing cutaway. Inside a case it can hand Isaac the answer his PC hunts; the table questionnaire sets cutaways in general. Samples: a roleplay turn's close, present tense, in a Draw Board gauge-house (where a district's draw is metered) where the clerk Pell died at his book.

options.label: No cut in his case
options.consequence: While his PC works a case, no cutaway touches it; the turn ends on what he can see. Cutaways stay legal for every other Front.
options.sample: The gauge book lies open under the lamp where Pell's cheek last rested on it. Every entry runs the same brown-black down the column, draughts and hours in a clerk's square hand, until the last line, which is grey. *Housing sound. Seal entire.* On the brass housing behind the desk the Board's seal stands a little proud of the slate, and under the reek of lamp oil there is a smell of hot wax that ought to have gone cold a day ago.

options.label: Cut to the hand
options.consequence: A turn may close on a short marked cut to the other side moving (a hand, a room, a deed) that may carry a clue, never a face, a name or the answer.
options.sample:
The last line in the gauge book is grey where every line above it has gone brown-black. *Housing sound. Seal entire.*

*Two streets over.* A gloved hand writes *Seal entire* on a sheet of scrap in a clerk's square hand, and again below it, and again, until the last could pass a Board audit. Then it feeds the sheet to the stove a corner at a time and holds the poker on the ash until it breaks.

options.label: Cut freely
options.consequence: Current law kept inside a case (R49-09): a cutaway may name the culprit and show his reasons, and Isaac plays his PC's ignorance as an actor does.
options.sample:
The last line in the gauge book is grey where every line above it has gone brown-black. *Housing sound. Seal entire.*

*Two streets over.* Orrin Vass, Board inspector for the Cutler Row split, feeds the stove a sheet of scrap a corner at a time. Twenty lines of *Seal entire* curl brown in a clerk's square hand, and the last of them could pass an audit. *Ash keeps no hand,* he thinks, and holds the poker on it until it breaks.

questions.rec_reason: It is the shape he chose for ambushes a day ago (R71-52): it keeps the Front moving and the dread live, can plant a fair clue, and leaves the solve with Isaac (R71-6).

sections.title: Mystery and investigation
sections.intro: How a case is built, worked and closed: clue counts and records, false leads and the fail state, the Night Watch on the page, interrogation, witnesses, lies and instruments, the investigator's head, the solution and the reveal, and the Watch at the table.

questions.title: Clues per conclusion
questions.question: How many clues must point to each conclusion a case needs reached?
questions.context: Nothing rules it. Justin Alexander's Three Clue Rule (from tabletop practice) plants at least three for every conclusion, because players miss, misread and forget. R71-23 shows a fighting tell twice and reads it at the third. The archive's clues come by three roads: the room, a mouth, and paper.

options.label: Three, by three roads
options.consequence: At least three clues per conclusion: one in the room, one in a mouth, one on paper or an instrument, so no single kind of looking is required. The notes list all three.

options.label: Three, any road
options.consequence: At least three clues per conclusion, by whatever roads the case offers; the notes list them.

options.label: Two sightings
options.consequence: R71-23 extended to investigation: each conclusion's clue shows plainly twice before it can be read, and one road is enough.

options.label: One clear clue
options.consequence: One clue per conclusion, placed fairly; the case is a test, and missing it is a real failure.

questions.rec_reason: The house's clues already live in rooms, mouths and ledgers, and three roads let Isaac solve by his PC's strengths instead of by Natalie's favourite door.

questions.title: Where the truth is kept
questions.question: Which records does every open mystery keep?
questions.context: The truth behind each open mystery is scattered across villain-POV scenes, cards and CONTINUITY.md. The night-watch book tracks 32 hooks, but the Kharven thread's oil lamp, burn-salve and one-word letter sit in no Front, Ledger line or bible. R71-30's planted-sign list covers fights only.

options.label: A sealed truth file
options.consequence: One entry per open mystery under table/: who, how, why, what each NPC knows, what stays kept. Natalie reads it each session; play never quotes it. One file with any sealed Front file.

options.label: Clue list in the notes
options.consequence: Every scene's author notes list each clue planted, found or missed, and the conclusion it serves, so fairness can be audited after.

options.label: A clue column on Fronts
options.consequence: Each mystery's Front carries planted, found and missed clue lines beside its Want and Next move.

options.label: Ledger's who-knows-what
options.consequence: The Ledger's existing 'who knows what' section gains a line for every PC-facing secret, with its due condition.

questions.rec_reason: A gives K2's sealed solution a home and B makes every scene auditable; the Ledger and the Fronts already carry enough, and a third copy drifts.

questions.title: Red herrings
questions.question: Are red herrings (false leads planted on purpose) legal, and what may they be built from?
questions.context: R49-36 governs lies, and R12-4 makes a confident wrong explanation 'the most valuable tool in the kit'. Fair-play writers from Christie on build false leads from true facts pointing the wrong way; a planted object no reader could refute breaks fair play. No WOTR rule names them.

options.label: None at all
options.consequence: Every planted clue points true; misdirection comes only from what the POV fails to weigh and from NPC lies, which already owe a tell.

options.label: True facts, refutable
options.consequence: A herring is built from true facts that point the wrong way, is refutable on the page, and is listed as a herring in the notes.

options.label: Wrong theories only
options.consequence: The only false leads are NPCs' confident wrong theories (R12-4); no object or document is planted to mislead.

options.label: Any lead, refuted later
options.consequence: A herring may be false in itself (a planted object, a staged room) so long as the solution refutes it; the notes still list it.

questions.rec_reason: It is the fair-play method, it gives veteran-clever NPCs (R48-36) room to frame someone with real things, and the notes keep it auditable.

questions.title: When the clues are missed
questions.question: If a case's clues go unread, what happens?
questions.context: R71-8 promises every fight 'at least one findable line out'; nothing says what a missed case does. Tabletop designers warn against the dead end, a case that stalls for good when one clue is missed. R71-101 already puts an unread killing on the Ledger as a risk.

options.label: The culprit wins
options.consequence: A missed case lets its Front resolve against his PC; the world moves on and the truth stays in the file.

options.label: A second road opens
options.consequence: The world moves and opens a new route: another body, a letter, a witness who comes forward. The case stays solvable at no extra cost.

options.label: Both, at a price
options.consequence: The Front ticks and a costlier road opens: each miss spends something (a witness, a Trace read once, a life), so the case stays solvable and the delay shows on the Ledger.

questions.rec_reason: Grimdark charges for every miss, and a case that can always be solved for a price keeps the table moving without ever being rigged.

questions.title: The rest of a Watch search
questions.question: Beyond the residue reading the combat law rules, how does a Night Watch search of a room, a body or a seal read on the page?
questions.context: R71-81 rules the residue reading: 'Protocol as action', figures read aloud; Isaac passed over field-book lines set into the scene. Nothing rules the rest of a search. The Night Watch page gives a coil walked along a wall and tins sealed standing under chapter wax. Samples: written scene, past tense; a coil-carrier searches the gauge-house where the Draw Board's clerk died.

options.label: Every search as protocol
options.consequence: R71-81 extends to every Watch search: rooms, bodies and seals play step by step as action, figures in a mouth, nothing summarised.
options.sample: Quail read ambient at the door and said it aloud, and Pegg wrote it on his cuff. Then she walked the coil along the slate at chest height, her eyes on the wire. It lay quiet past the meter and past the stopcock. At the brass housing it leaned, and she held it there and read the needle out again. Pegg had the tin open before she asked. She scraped the Board's seal with her nail-knife, and the wax came away in two layers, an old red under a newer one.

options.label: Instruments only as protocol
options.consequence: Instrument work plays as R71-81's protocol; the rest of the room arrives as the carrier's noticing in her culture's order (R70-44), with empty corners passed in a line.
options.sample: Quail took the room floor first, as carriers are taught: lamp oil soaked into the boards by the desk, the clerk's stool pushed back, the gauge book open under the lamp. None of it wanted the coil. The brass housing did, because the Board's seal on it stood a little proud of the slate. There she read ambient aloud, and Pegg wrote it on his cuff. She scraped the seal with her nail-knife, and the wax came away in two layers, an old red under a newer one.

options.label: Protocol, closed on filing
options.consequence: As A, and the search closes on its docket line set off from the prose: the Register's flat record against the long hour, the Lord of the Mysteries document turned to a close.
options.sample:
At the brass housing the coil leaned, and Quail held it there and read the needle out again while Pegg wrote. She scraped the Board's seal with her nail-knife, and the wax came away in two layers, an old red under a newer one. Pegg sealed the scrape in its tin standing, and they walked back to Cutler Row without speaking.

*Exhibit C, Cutler Row split. Wax from the housing seal, two layers. Taken standing. Assay of record: Quail, H.*

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the action he chose for readings, carries it through the whole search, and the flat filing after a long hour is the Night Register's own voice and the Lord of the Mysteries register he picked.

questions.title: The interrogation
questions.question: How does a questioning read when the witness is lying?
questions.context: The archive has reports and councils but no interrogation written out; Josse Hillborn's runs two sentences. R71-22 makes a lie inside a fight a move with a price. Hilary Mantel's Cromwell (Wolf Hall) makes every courtesy a threat. Samples: written scene, past tense; a Society man questions the lamp boy who found the body, and the boy lies about the hour.

options.label: A duel of tells
options.consequence: R71-22's accounting extends past fights: each question aims at a tell, and the page shows what it bought or cost.
options.sample:
"When did the hum stop?"

"Third hour. Same as always." Tam said it before the question was done.

Pegg turned his own lamp up so the boy's hands showed: lamp-black on the fingers, as there should be, and a new copper turning over and over in the right one. "Then you lit the Row twice," he said, "since your can's half empty and it's a short row." The coin stopped. That bought him the boy's eyes, and cost him the boy's mouth for the rest of the night.

options.label: The quiet interview
options.consequence: Courtesy is the threat, Mantel's way: the questioner asks after the witness's life, writes the lie down as if true, and the reader feels what went unsaid.
options.sample: Pegg gave the boy the stool and took the step himself, so that Tam had to look up at him. He asked after Tam's mother, and her chest, and whether the Board had cut her plate yet for the arrears. Tam said not yet. Pegg said that was a mercy, the Board being slow in a cold quarter. Then he asked when the hum had stopped, and Tam said the third hour, same as always, and Pegg wrote it down in his good hand and thanked him.

options.label: Summary, then the line
options.consequence: The archive's habit kept: the questioning is summarised, and only the line that matters is played, with its tell.
options.sample:
Pegg had the boy on the step for most of an hour and got the shape of the night out of him: the lamps on the Row, oil because the main was down, the gauge-house door standing open, Pell at his book with his cheek on the page. Tam told it twice and both tellings matched. At the end Pegg asked when the hum had stopped.

"Third hour," Tam said. "Same as always."

He said it before Pegg had finished asking.

questions.rec_reason: It is the interrogation the archive has never written, it gives Isaac's PC a fair read of every tell, and it matches the combat law he has just ruled.

questions.title: Clue objects
questions.question: Which objects carry the clues, case to case?
questions.context: The archive's best clues are priced in the economy: oil where tallow burns, a salve too good for the kitchen, a grain date that does not fit. But lamps, wax and ledgers lead nearly every case. R70-44 already gives each Standing Inventory a 'Notices first' line.

options.label: Keep the house signature
options.consequence: Lamps, wax, seals and ledgers stay the leading clue beds in every culture, the Draw Age's paperwork as every case's spine.

options.label: By culture
options.consequence: Each Standing Inventory gains a 'Clue beds' line beside 'Notices first': Kharven counts and the woodpile, Accord meters and wax, Moto seals and court verse. A case draws its clues from its culture.

options.label: Rotate per case
options.consequence: No clue object leads two cases running in one thread; the notes log which objects led, and the next case picks another.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps money-before-magic detection fair to anyone who reads the Inventory, and it breaks the lamp-and-wax habit without banning it.

questions.title: The investigator's head
questions.question: When the POV is the investigator, how much of her thinking does the reader get?
questions.context: R70-38 allows both numbered steps in italic thought and 'the unsaid'. Knox's eighth rule bars a detective from using a clue the reader was not shown; only the Watson (the slower friend) must voice every thought. Samples: written scene, past tense; the coil-carrier finds the dead clerk's last line in fresher ink (iron-gall ink writes pale and darkens over hours as it oxidises).

options.label: The notice withheld
options.consequence: She may notice what the page withholds; the reader sees her act on it and learns why at the solution. Legal under R70-38's unsaid, unfair by Knox's eighth.
options.sample: Quail turned the gauge book to the lamp and read down the column slowly, and when she reached the foot of it she read the last line again. She stood a while with one finger on the margin beside it. Pegg coughed. She closed the book without marking the page and asked him who held the Board's seal press for the Cutler Row split.

options.label: Every step aloud
options.consequence: Every inference reaches the page as she makes it, in numbered italic thought (R70-38); the reader always knows what the investigator thinks.
options.sample: The last line was grey where every line above it had gone brown-black. *One: iron-gall writes pale and darkens in the air, a night to go black. Two: the column above is a night old. Three: so this line went in hours after the rest, perhaps after his cheek was on the page. Four: someone wrote Seal entire in his hand.* She closed the book and asked Pegg who held the Board's seal press for the Cutler Row split.

options.label: Facts shown, conclusion held
options.consequence: Every fact she notices reaches the page plainly; the conclusion waits, carried by her next act, as Holmes keeps his. Numbered steps stay legal at the solution.
options.sample: Every line in the column had gone the brown-black that iron-gall goes when it has had a night in the air. The last line was grey. *Housing sound. Seal entire.* Quail tipped the book toward the lamp and the grey stayed grey, and the sour smell of fresh ink still came off the page. She closed it and asked Pegg who held the Board's seal press for the Cutler Row split.

questions.rec_reason: It meets Knox and keeps Kawabata's unsaid, so the reader races the investigator on equal facts, and the stepwise list pays off at the solution as Death Note's reasoning does.

questions.title: How witnesses err
questions.question: When a witness is wrong without lying, how is the error built?
questions.context: The roster files honest errors and lies under one 'lied about' field (Josse Osricsson's believed error sits there). Elizabeth Loftus's eyewitness research shows real patterns: short events remembered as long, the weapon remembered over the face, details planted by a leading question. R70-44 already lets a culture misread a room.

options.label: As memory really errs
options.consequence: Each witness's honest error follows real memory science, and a careful questioner can find it by the pattern.

options.label: As their culture misreads
options.consequence: Each witness misreads by his Standing Inventory and folk belief (R70-44 and R53-15 extended to testimony).

options.label: Both, logged apart
options.consequence: Errors come by either road, and the roster gains an 'errs about' field beside 'lied about', so an honest error never owes a liar's tell.

questions.rec_reason: Isaac wants real science and culture-keyed worlds both, and splitting error from lie keeps R49-36's tell owed only where someone chose to deceive.

questions.title: The lie never caught
questions.question: What becomes of a lie his PC never catches?
questions.context: Table Rule 8 keeps a wrong statement 'uncorrected until he catches it' and stops there. Joan Aldery's nail in the Rovhen run still stands, unnoticed. Apocalypse World (the tabletop game WOTR's Fronts come from) turns an ignored warning into a hard move, the blow that lands on a missed chance.

options.label: It stands
options.consequence: The lie is the world as his PC knows it. If never caught it never costs him; the truth stays in the files.

options.label: It comes due
options.consequence: The first time his PC acts on it, the lie opens a Ledger line; the truth arrives as that line's cost when it bites, the tell already behind him to find.

options.label: A Front carries it
options.consequence: A lie that matters is tied to a Front; the truth surfaces when that Front ticks, whatever he does.

options.label: Told at arc's end
options.consequence: An uncaught lie stands in play, and the arc's closing State of Play names it to Isaac, so the author learns what his PC never did.

questions.rec_reason: Grimdark wants the bill: a missed lie that costs nothing is decoration, and billing it when he acts on it ties the cost to his own choice, never to a timer.

questions.title: What instruments prove
questions.question: Can an instrument's reading be wrong in a case?
questions.context: R70-78: 'instruments still read everyone else', and R71-44 prints a faculty's figures exact 'unless warded'. The Night Watch page: a clean assay means only that nothing signed above the Bureau's floor. Umineko's 'red truth' (a statement the story guarantees true) makes a mystery fair by fixing some facts beyond doubt.

options.label: Never lies, may miss
options.consequence: A sound instrument prints true. A case lives in what one was not built to read: below its floor, behind a ward, or asked the wrong question. The notes say which.

options.label: May be wrong, findably
options.consequence: Calibration drift and tampering exist; every wrong reading is findable by the chapter bench's standard or a second instrument, and R71-84's forgery law covers instruments too.

questions.rec_reason: It gives every case a floor of hard truth to reason from, matches the Watch's own creed, and makes the cheat a matter of what was asked, which is fairer and stranger.

questions.title: The solution scene
questions.question: Which forms may a case's solution scene take?
questions.context: A drawing-room summation is one long voice, held to R48-43's one crafted speech outside court and R19-4's ban on telling people what they both know. Ace Attorney (a courtroom game) turns where a statement meets the exhibit that contradicts it, as R71-81 turns on instruments that disagree. Whether the court itself can be bought is IN7's question.

options.label: The summation
options.consequence: One voice lays out the case to the room, spending the scene's crafted speech (R48-43); the room must not already know what it hears.

options.label: The hearing
options.consequence: A court, inquest or Register hearing, turned where a statement meets the exhibit that breaks it; each culture keeps its own justice (R53-11).

options.label: The procedure
options.consequence: A test or instrument proves it on the page as action (R71-81), and the result is the verdict.

options.label: The document
options.consequence: The case closes as a filing, a docket or a set-off notice (R70-67, R70-17), its last line the verdict.

questions.rec_reason: A drawing room needs the suspects gathered for no reason the world supplies; the hearing gives the same speech a legal reason to happen, and his chancery world with instruments solves through the other two.

questions.title: The reveal
questions.question: How does the answer land on the page?
questions.context: R70-20 lets reveals run as clustered one-line paragraphs; Junji Ito holds a reveal for the page turn and draws it calm and complete. Samples: written scene, past tense; the coil-carrier proves the Board inspector sealed the dead clerk's gauge-housing twice in one night.

options.label: Cold, in a cluster
options.consequence: The answer lands as a short cluster of one-line paragraphs at the moment of proof; the explanation comes later or never.
options.sample:
Quail laid the scraped wax on Vass's bench and lowered his die onto it.

It went home.

Every ridge of the Board's arms sat in the old red, and the new wax over it had taken the same die a hair off true, the way a seal takes a hurried hand.

Orrin Vass had sealed the Cutler Row housing twice in one night, and only one of those was in his book.

options.label: The chain walked back
options.consequence: The investigator lays the chain out link by link, each planted clue named, as for a hearing; the reader checks it against what he saw.
options.sample: Quail set it out for the Warden as she would for a hearing. The ferrule at the split ran wider than the standard bore, so the house had drawn more than its book billed for as long as nobody measured it. The wax came off in two layers. Someone had struck the seal twice. Pell's last line was grey, hours younger than the rest, and it said the seal was entire. One man on the split carried the Board's die. She put Vass's press on the desk.

options.label: The object, then silence
options.consequence: The proof is a thing done in the room; nobody explains, and the chain reaches the reader in the next scene's docket or not at all.
options.sample: The press was in the second drawer of Vass's bench, wrapped in a shammy that smelled of brass polish and hot wax. Quail unwrapped it without a word, turned the die to the lamp, and pressed it into the scrape of new wax from the Cutler Row housing. It went home to the last ridge. Vass looked at it for a long moment and then sat down on his own stool, carefully, like a man who had just been told the price of something.

questions.rec_reason: Isaac's own reversals land as the record overturned in a line, R70-20 already licenses the cluster, and the full chain has its natural home in the hearing or docket that follows.

questions.title: The Watch at the table
questions.question: What is the Night Watch to a live thread?
questions.context: No live thread carries a Watch character. The Watch holds the crown's warrant, prints its walkers' names on every insert, and in Ketsuen a Searcher (a Watch investigator) 'can ask and cannot compel' (R67-4). R70-97 already gives contract hooks a reward and a penalty.

options.label: A patron with contracts
options.consequence: The Register posts closed filings as contracts with a fee and a penalty (R70-97); his PC may take one, and the Watch's file follows him after.

options.label: A rival office
options.consequence: The Watch files on what PCs do (unlicensed high working, undeclared killings) and arrives as a Front when they do it.

options.label: Both, by where
options.consequence: Patron where the crown's warrant runs and his PC is neither the hand (who did it) nor the purse (who paid); rival where he is either. In Ketsuen it can only ask.

options.label: Book lens only
options.consequence: The Watch stays in written work; a live thread meets it only as news in the Rumor Mill.

questions.rec_reason: The Watch's own law decides which face it shows, which is fair and findable, and it gives every thread a standing mystery engine without a Watch PC.

questions.title: Naming Malphas in a file
questions.question: May a Night Watch file name Malphas, now that he signs the Necrocursica in his own name?
questions.context: C-125, open: the night-watch book's rule that no file names him binds the Farrant Papers (R61-62), yet he signs the Necrocursica 'in his own name' (R61-49), and the Codex volumes the Papers hold as exhibits name him. The published Papers take the strict reading.

options.label: Title only, everywhere
options.consequence: No Watch file names him; he is filed by his title at his own written request, and named volumes are read at the desk, never copied in. The Papers stand.

options.label: Named as author only
options.consequence: A file may cite the Necrocursica by its signed author, as a bibliography line; no file connects that author to a case's hand, so the book's spine holds.

options.label: Files name him freely
options.consequence: The book's rule narrows to Wystan Ashmore's own case file; every other Watch record may name him.

questions.rec_reason: It is what the published Papers already do, so nothing published changes, a villain choosing his own filing name is canon character, and the night-watch book's rule that neither man learns of the other stays whole.

settled.point: Big surprises (betrayal, ambush, death) come only after foreshadowing a player could have caught, and a loss shows a sign and an exit first.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; this questionnaire extends it to cases through K2 and MY1, and to schemes and betrayals through IN2 and IN3, rather than reopening it.

settled.point: A wrong conclusion is well reasoned, and the confident wrong explanation is the main tool of misdirection.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; MY3 builds red herrings on it.

settled.point: Folk beliefs stand uncorrected by narration, and the POV's culture decides what he makes of a room, misreadings included.
settled.why_not_asked: Style law and older live law; MY7 and MY9 extend them to clue beds and testimony, and HO5 asks only whether events may settle a belief about the dead.

settled.point: Natalie places the tell and never draws the deduction for Isaac's PC; a tell shows plainly twice and is read at the third.
settled.why_not_asked: Combat law K9 and CW14, ruled 2026-10-04; K6 and MY1 build the table's clue economy on them.

settled.point: A held reveal may act early as evidence a reader could catch, with the notes listing each planted sign; the deciding fact shows beforehand; every fight has a findable way out.
settled.why_not_asked: Combat law MC4, K6 and K7; K2 carries the principle from fights to cases.

settled.point: A turn may close on a short marked cutaway, and in roleplay an ambush's shooter half is one turn's closing cutaway with the shot in the next.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law and combat law FT2; K7 asks only whether a cutaway may touch a case his PC is working, the table questionnaire sets cutaways in general, and IN6 asks only what a Front's file shows Isaac.

settled.point: Secrets reach the page through the four explaining voices, at most two per engagement; the document voice sets a rule the scene then breaks.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled by Isaac in Pack Twelve; MY5 and MY12 use the document voice as given.

settled.point: The narrator foreshadows only in a chapter's opening and closing lines and never winks at the reader who knows better; a scene may open on a document it then tests, a chapter on an in-world epigraph, and a scene may close by breaking off before the payoff.
settled.why_not_asked: Style law, ruled 2026-10-03; HO1 paces dread inside the POV lock.

settled.point: In-world documents may be lists and notebooks, records of the strange, court annals and memorials, or Guild reference entries.
settled.why_not_asked: Style law; MY5 and MY12 ask only where documents sit in a case, and HO7 and HO8 offer them as options.

settled.point: A reasoning POV may set out numbered steps in italic thought, or leave the conclusion unsaid.
settled.why_not_asked: Both are legal by the style law; MY8 asks only which is fair for an investigator's POV.

settled.point: A 'What nobody knows' question is never answered as fact; Epoch-scale things make dread and never resolve a plot.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; a case solves a person's act, never the world's own mysteries, and HO7 asks only how close Epoch-scale things come to the page.

settled.point: A residue reading plays as protocol in action with figures read aloud, the instruments' contradiction its turn (field-book lines set in were passed over); poisons are proved by the period's real tests where the gradient puts them.
settled.why_not_asked: Combat law AL12 and AL11; MY5 asks only about the rest of a search.

settled.point: A forgery is always findable by mark, assay or the Index's own failure; a corrupt alchemist shows one planted sign a scene; an impression-body leaks a seam the reader can catch.
settled.why_not_asked: Combat law AL15, AL13 and AL18; IN7 asks whether a bought court or a lost file follows the forgery rule.

settled.point: Law moves on proof (a witness or a reading inside the residue clocks); every practitioner's killing opens a jurisdiction contest as a Front; an undeclared killing by next dawn is murder; each culture keeps its own justice.
settled.why_not_asked: Combat law WT12 and older live law; MY12 asks only the solution scene's form, and IN7 only whether the process can be bought.

settled.point: The Night Watch is a crown-chartered society with walkers, coil-carriers, a bulletin office and the Night Register; residue runs on two clocks and every Anamnesis read spends the Trace it reads.
settled.why_not_asked: Canon; MY14 asks only the Watch's place at a live thread.

settled.point: Meta knowledge informs Natalie and never rigs an engagement either way; the partner explains physics only when asked.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; K2's sealed solution rests on it.

settled.point: A faculty's read delivers a bare fact, never an interpretation; a faculty reads exact unless the target is warded; instruments read everyone but the bearer.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law; MY11 asks only whether an instrument may be wrong.

settled.point: Court cultures argue in long formal speech at court; outside court one crafted speech at a big moment; nobody explains what both already know.
settled.why_not_asked: Style law and live law; MY12 builds the solution scene inside them.

settled.point: Every hook offered at the table states its reward and penalty, as a Guild or Crown contract.
settled.why_not_asked: Style law; MY14 asks only whether the Watch posts such contracts.

settled.point: Every public reversal or face-slap opens a Front or a Ledger debt; comedy may sit hard against dread, each played straight, with only gallows wit inside danger.
settled.why_not_asked: Style law, ruled 2026-10-03.
